building.name: Heritage on the Marina
building.completed_conflict: This building is dated 1925 in the historical record; the assessor's roll gives the parcel a build year of 1924.

historical_record.description: Kate F. Austin, a property investor and widow of merchant Henry S. Austin, acquired the whole block (then Western Addition Block 184) and had it graded.

The site held part of a work camp of contractors Warren & Malley, who built the seawall and filled the Marina: two stables and a store room on the southern half and a carpenter's shop at the Laguna and Bay corner.
After the 1906 earthquake the block was cut into small house lots and leased to H.M. Wooley, who moved 75 refugee cottages onto it from the Lobos Square refugee camp in late 1906 or early 1907.
The San Francisco Board of Health resolved to condemn the refugee-cottage settlement on the block, claiming the cottages lacked running water and toilets.
The block was leased to the Panama-Pacific International Exposition Company, ending the refugee-cottage settlement.
A Superior Court judge ordered the Board of Health to show cause for its condemnation of the refugee cottages on the block, finding they had kitchens and bathrooms.

During the Panama-Pacific International Exposition the block lay in the Zone amusement area, holding the "Incubator Babies" exhibit, part of the Santa Fe Railroad's "Indian Pueblo," and parts of "The Submarines" and "Toyland Grown Up."
With the exposition grounds cleared, the block was returned to its owner, who left it undeveloped.
The Ladies' Protection and Relief Society bought the entire block bounded by Bay, Octavia, Francisco and Laguna streets.
The Society resurveyed the block, kept its western two-thirds, and sold most of the eastern third.
The Heritage on the Marina, designed by architect Julia Morgan.
The building was designed as the San Francisco Ladies' Protection and Relief Society's home, in the Tudor Revival style.

Construction began in spring 1924, funded in part by a $50,000 bequest from the estate of the late Lizzie G. Hovey; a $2,500 gift from Serena Goodall Keil paid for the rear gardens, named Serena Court.
The Society filed for and received the building permit for a $140,000 three-story-over-basement building with a steel and concrete frame and load-bearing brick walls.
Built in 1925 as an institutional building, now Heritage on the Marina.
Photographed, showing the Ladies' Protection & Relief Society.
The original gardens and landscaping were designed by Arthur A. Smith, apparently with input from Golden Gate Park superintendent John McLaren.
The home opened as a short-term convalescent home for women recovering from illness or surgery, also taking a few retired women for life; care and board cost $1 a day.
The completed home and gardens were opened for public inspection.
A $4,000 rooftop sunroom with two elevator overrides, designed by Julia Morgan as part of her original plan, was built on the garden side of the roof by contractor N.F. Nielsen.
A one-story stone cottage for the head groundskeeper, costing $2,000, was designed and built at the northeast corner of the site, apparently from reused street cobbles.

The Society sold the northwest corner of the property to the City, under a condemnation order, for a WPA project widening Bay Street to four lanes; the fence was rebuilt on the new line and Monterey pines were planted at the corner.
The Society marked its ninetieth anniversary here, still caring for convalescent women and housing retired women.
A one-story, wood-frame garden house costing $3,000 was built on the grounds.
The Society marked its centennial; residents over 65 paid $55 a month for room, board and medical care.
The Society agreed to merge with the Crocker Old People's Home and consolidate both at this site, keeping its own name and admitting men for the first time.
The Planning Commission approved rezoning the parcel from residential to commercial so a senior guest home addition could be built.

A permit was sought for a $510,000 reinforced-concrete residential addition behind the original building, designed by Warren C. Perry with structural engineer Thomas E. Chace and built by Erbentraut and Summers; it became known as the Perry Building.
Photographed, showing the Ladies' Protection & Relief Society.
A further story, also designed by Warren Perry, was added to the addition while under construction, bringing the project to just over a million dollars.
The stone groundskeeper's cottage was remodelled into a superintendent's residence for $2,000, to designs by architect Hewitt C. Wells.
The expanded home was formally dedicated as a nonprofit, non-sectarian residence for older men and women, with 100 private rooms, a 16-bed infirmary and a 50-seat chapel.
The expanded retirement home took the name "The Heritage."
The Heritage was threatened with losing its tax exemption for charging over $150 a month without sufficient on-site medical care.
Construction began in late summer on a $160,000 one-story infirmary designed by Gardner Dailey and built by Swinerton & Walberg, now the Health Care Center.
The Planning Commission unanimously approved a new infirmary south of the original building on condition it be one story only.
Gardner Dailey designed a $96,000 interior remodel of the Perry Building, converting the former infirmary space into residential units and adding bathrooms.
The one-story infirmary was finished; its certificate of final inspection followed on September 23, 1963.
Landscape architect Casey Kawamoto was hired to design the Central Courtyard, redesign the Rear Courtyard and relandscape the perimeter in a modernist vocabulary.
Photographed.
A new sprinkler system and other mechanical upgrades were installed.
The Society marked its 125th anniversary; the home then housed 104 people with an average age of 85.
Architect Warren C. Perry, designer of the 1957 addition, died here aged 95.
Two Postmodern additions referencing the original building's Jacobethan styling were built on the north and west sides of the Health Care Clinic, designed by Spencer & Associates.
After Loma Prieta earthquake damage, three masonry fireplaces and three chimneys were removed from the Morgan Building.
Replicas of the original chimneys were built on the Morgan Building.
A steel-frame, corrugated-metal loading dock was added on the north side of the Morgan Building.
The Heritage was renamed Heritage on the Marina.
Community members nominated the property for Article 10 landmark designation.
The Historic Preservation Commission initiated landmark designation of the property (Resolution No. 1416).
The Historic Preservation Commission recommended landmark designation of the property (Resolution No. 1425).
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 320, Ladies' Protection and Relief Society.
